title: The days slip by
hookLine: the early saloks warn that days slip away while the mind sleeps (Salok M9, ang 1426)

lines: A PHOTO FROM FIVE YEARS AGO.
BUSY CAN BE A KIND OF SLEEP.
cards: Look at a photo from five years ago. The haircut, the phone in your hand, the people beside you. Some you still see.
Some you haven't spoken to in years. Where did those five years go? You were there for every day, and yet most of them left no trace.
You weren't asleep. You were busy. But busy can be its own kind of sleep.
The early saloks of Guru Tegh Bahadur keep coming back to this, couplet after couplet, like someone gently shaking a sleeper's shoulder.

teach.b: The second salok asks, in paraphrase: why are you so absorbed in poisonous things? You don't turn away from them even for an instant. Says Nanak, meditate on the Lord, O mind, and you won't be caught in death's noose.

teach.h: NIMAKH: ONE BLINK OF AN EYE.
teach.b: The word for instant is nimakh, the blink of an eye. The salok isn't asking for a whole life of retreat. It asks: could you look up, even for one blink?

The third salok ends with a line that sums up this whole run: your lifespan is passing, slipping away. Auadh is the span of life, the time you were given. And it's going, right now, at exactly the speed of this sentence.
Listen to how the saloks repeat themselves.

teach.h: KAHO NAANAK: A REFRAIN THAT WAKES.
teach.b: Again and again, the second line begins kaho naanak, says Nanak, and then calls the mind: O mind, man re, manaa. They're built like a refrain, and the repetition is the teaching.
A single warning is forgotten by lunchtime. A couplet that keeps coming back, at the end of every reading, wears a groove in you. And notice what they don't say.
They don't say the days are bad, or that time spent working or loving is wasted.
They say the days slip, and the mind sleeps through them. The cure isn't more hours. It's waking up inside the ones you have, even for the blink of an eye.

how: Sikhs hear the ninth Guru's saloks at the close of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib; many know their refrain, kaho naanak, by heart, and take them as reminders that life's time is passing.

o: the blink of an eye, an instant
the span of life you were given
a refrain sung at a hymn's end

games.q: the days slip by — tap the pairs.

s: the saloks say time spent working or loving is wasted
they say the days slip while the mind sleeps; the cure is waking inside them.
the second salok asks the mind to turn away even for an instant
nimakh, the blink of an eye, is enough to begin.
many saloks repeat the same opening to their second line
kaho naanak, says Nanak, then a call to the mind.

games.q: the saloks say your lifespan is slipping away. what do they ask of the mind?
o: a whole life of retreat from the world.
to wake and remember, even for a blink.
to fill every hour with more tasks.
games.why: the second salok asks why the mind won't turn away even for an instant, nimakh, and says meditate on the Lord, O mind.

practice: Look at a clock and say the time to yourself, then the date, the day of the week, and where you are.

Close your eyes and let each breath be a blink of waking, a nimakh; when you drift into plans or replays, come back to the clock's simple fact: it's now. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths.

wordCard.voice: Auadh, the span of life. Guru Tegh Bahadur's early saloks warn that it is slipping away, and ask the mind to wake even for a blink.

carryVoice: Your line: the days slip. One awake blink is enough to begin. Five hundred ninety days, and counting.

sources.ref: Salok Mahalla 9, saloks 2–3 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1426)
